_schema.description: Kaplan 2025 'SHSAT Practice Tests and Explanations' book, Practice Test 2, Part 1 ELA, questions 1-10 (Revising/Editing Part A, standalone items 1-5; Revising/Editing Part B, passage-based items 6-10). Questions/options transcribed verbatim from the book. Explanations are NOT transcribed as text per the user's instruction — each question's 'Solution' button shows a cropped photo of the book's 'Getting to the Answer' explanation instead.
_schema.source: Kaplan SHSAT Practice Tests and Explanations, Practice Test 2, pages 404-409 (questions) and 443-444 (answers/explanations)
_schema.status: Questions 1-14 and 58-114 transcribed (of 114 total: 14 ELA + 57 math) — that's all the Revising/Editing section (Part A+B). Reading Comprehension questions 15-57 are blocked: those passage pages were never photographed, only pages 404-410 (Revising/Editing) and 430-439 (Math) were uploaded.
_schema.option_letters: The book alternates A-D and E-H per question (standard test-booklet convention to avoid bubble-sheet confusion) — preserved exactly as printed rather than normalized.

standalone_items.stimulus: (1) A talented geographer, the professor, who teaches college students, is an expert at locating cities and countries on maps. (2) In his lectures, he explains cartography, or map-making, which involves surveying the Earth's surface to represent its physical structures. (3) Geographers use maps with different projections that can display the Earth's various features, including mountains, the magnetic poles, and oceans. (4) Studying the field of geography provides knowledge about its connections to biology, sociology, and history, among other subjects.
standalone_items.question: Which sentence should be revised to correct a wordiness issue?

standalone_items.stimulus: (1) After graduating from college, the next five years of a software engineer's life are spent working toward a graduate degree in computer science. (2) The coursework revolves around programming, which is the preparation of instructions that tell the computer which operations it needs to perform. (3) Students learn formulas as well as programs that translate complex computer languages. (4) With new advancements every day, the computer science field requires professionals to constantly learn about applying the latest technology.
standalone_items.question: Which sentence contains an error in its construction and should be revised?

standalone_items.stimulus: The federal government <u>provides</u> low-interest loans that <u>allow</u> students <u>of deferring</u> payment until they graduate and <u>begin to</u> work.
standalone_items.question: Which edit should be made to correct this sentence?

standalone_items.stimulus: The helicopter, <u>which offers</u> the advantages of flight without requiring <u>large amounts of space</u> for <u>takeoff and landing</u>, <u>allowing</u> relatively easy access to places as remote as islands, mountain villages, and snow-bound communities.
standalone_items.question: Which edit should be made to correct the sentence?

options.F: Change **large amounts of space** to **space in large amounts**.
options.G: Change **takeoff and landing** to **the takeoff as well as the landing**.

standalone_items.stimulus: (1) New York state has more than 70,000 miles of rivers and streams. (2) One of New York's rivers is the Hudson River. (3) The Hudson River is home to dozens of rare birds and more than a hundred rare plants.
standalone_items.question: What is the best way to combine the sentences?

options.A: The Hudson River, one of New York's rivers, is home to dozens of rare birds and more than a hundred rare plants, and New York state has more than 70,000 miles of rivers and streams.
options.B: New York state has more than 70,000 miles of rivers and streams, and one of them is the Hudson River, which is home to dozens of rare birds and more than a hundred rare plants.
options.C: The Hudson River, home to dozens of rare birds and more than a hundred rare plants, is one of New York State's rivers, and New York state has more than 70,000 miles of rivers and streams.
options.D: New York state has more than 70,000 miles of rivers and streams, including the Hudson River, which is home to dozens of rare birds and more than a hundred rare plants.

sentence_paragraphs.text: Consciousness is a topic that has captivated psychologists since the beginning of experimental psychology in the late 1800s.
Wilhelm Wundt and William James, both notable founders of psychology, were fascinated with studying consciousness, both from the perspective of how it was organized and how it worked.
Consciousness refers to the active processing of information in the brain.
It is your awareness of yourself and your environment, and the features of your consciousness at any given point in time are referred to as your state of consciousness.
While in a normal state of consciousness, you are awake and alert.
In an altered state of consciousness, however, you experience a disruption to your normal state—such as falling asleep or drifting off into a daydream.
You may not realize that you experience different states of consciousness throughout each day.
You are likely not actively aware of your breathing, heartbeat, and other biological functions, for instance.
These body processes, which are being controlled by your brain, are happening on a nonconscious level.
According to psychoanalytic theory, all of the memories that you have stored and could actively start thinking about, if prompted, represent the preconscious level.
For example, what did you have for breakfast this morning?
Psychologists have found that people are affected by information that they are not aware of consciously.
This information is acting on a subconscious level.
According to Austrian psychologist Sigmund Freud, people possess subconscious longings that are often socially unacceptable.
Two examples that illustrate subconscious processing are priming and the mere-exposure effect.
Priming refers to the processing of information from stimuli that are outside of conscious awareness.
In fact, studies show that people can correctly answer questions that they have seen previously—even when they do not remember seeing the questions.
The mere-exposure effect happens when people prefer stimuli they have seen previously over new stimuli—even when they do not remember the old stimuli.
Psychologists design and conduct experiments that explore different states of consciousness to better understand how the brain processes information.
These experiments probe the inner workings of normal conscious, nonconscious, preconscious, and subconscious levels of being.

sentence_paragraphs.text: Handweaving, traditionally the province of home spinners and weavers, has been practiced throughout recorded history.
Silk weaving has been known in China since 3500 B.C.E and in Egypt since 3600 B.C.E.
By 700 C.E., looms were common in Africa, Asia, and Europe.
In particular, they were found throughout the Islamic world.
In mythology, weaving is typically the province of women.
In Pre-Dynastic Egypt, Neith was the goddess of weaving; in Greece, it was the goddess Athena; in Scandinavia, it was the goddess Frigg, the wife of chief god Odin.

These goddesses and other protectors of weavers show the importance of the craft to ancient peoples: each was not only prominent in her pantheon but also associated with other crucial domains, such as childbirth, wisdom, the creation of the stars, and fate itself.
Tales about weaving are numerous as well.
Theseus emerges from the maze of the Minotaur by following Ariadne's woven thread.
A crane weaves a gorgeous cloth of her own feathers as a gift for those who rescued her.
In the fable “The Old Man and Death,” Aesop warns of being careful of what you wish for.
Sleeping Beauty pricks her finger on a spindle and is cursed.
Indeed, the English word text derives from the Latin word textare—weaving, as in “weaving a story.”
Weaving continues to be an important part of many modern cultures as well.
In Ukraine, the rushnyk, a ritual cloth, accompanies people throughout their lives; a newborn is placed immediately upon it and the dead are covered with it.
Without question, the importance of weaving goes far beyond the practical into cultural meanings that still resonate today.
Navajo weaving often features the symbol of Spider Woman, who gave the art of weaving to Navajo women.
Andean peoples, living in close connection with nature, incorporate symbols for the sun and rivers.
A pattern or motif may be specific to the weaver herself and can convey piety, cultural or family traditions, daily life, folklore characters, and even humor.
